The registry is a single contract that links every registered name to its responsible resolver and lets the name owner change the resolver address or create subnames. A subname can have a different owner from its parent name. The resolver handles the actual resource lookup for a name and returns a contract address, content hash, IP address and so on. The registrar allocates names to users and is the only entity that can update ENS. In the registry, the owner of a node is that node's registrar. A registrar can be a contract or an externally owned account, but the root and top-level registrars are expected to be implemented at least as contracts. Name resolution has two steps. First, the name is hashed and the resolver address is obtained from the registry, and then the function matching the resource type is called on the resolver. As a result, granting such benefits requires issuing a separate new token, which is not bound to the original NFT. For example, if an airline distributes benefit tokens to attract CryptoPunks holders into its club, and the original NFT is later transferred to someone else, the benefit remains with the previous holder and the new holder does not automatically receive it. This standard proposes an interface that binds privileges to an NFT while still letting the holder manage and transfer each privilege independently.

However, as account abstraction has advanced, keys other than the secp256k1 that Ethereum natively supports have become widely used: the secp256r1 curve supported by many mobile devices, RSA keys issued by traditional institutions, and zero knowledge (ZK) schemes that sign with JWTs from email or large web services. However, blockchains and smart contracts are immutable once deployed, which makes this requirement hard to meet. In a complex system, when contracts reference each other in tangled relationships, bugs become easy to introduce and maintenance becomes difficult. If which contract uses which contract is scattered throughout the code, replacing one contract means hunting down and fixing every contract that holds its address. This standard solves the problem with two contracts: a registry that collects addresses in one place (ContractsRegistry) and a mixin that receives injected dependencies (Dependant). The stated advantages are a clear structure, the ability to add, remove, or replace contracts at runtime, upgrades that can be enabled when needed, and transparent dependency relationships.

If the metadata sits only on one server or one particular IPFS gateway, the information can be lost when that host goes down. A group with many subsidiaries and departments needs hierarchical key management, permission control and multi-signature mechanisms, but without a common rule each organization manages keys in its own way and permission boundaries between departments become blurred. Auditing is also hard, because there is no systematic way to trace which key belongs to which department. This standard defines how to derive subsidiary and department accounts from a single master key along a unified path, together with security requirements, and offers a solution that secures both assets and transaction efficiency in multi-chain environments.

If a function on the proxy collides with a function on the logic contract, the call is not forwarded to the logic contract and the proxy intercepts it and returns its own value. Citing the Nomic Labs article Malicious backdoors in Ethereum proxies, the original text explains that the compiler catches collisions within one contract but not between contracts, so collisions can be abused to hide a backdoor in a contract that looks normal. 1hwjjurrs1z: A regular account (EOA) transaction only needs its balance, nonce, and signature checked, and once a transaction is confirmed valid, it cannot become invalid without that account paying a fee. This makes mass-submission attacks economically infeasible, since costs spiral. Account abstraction, by contrast, performs validation using arbitrary EVM code that can depend on storage or block information. This makes it possible to craft a UserOperation that passes in the mempool but fails when included in a block, and a single storage change could invalidate huge numbers of unrelated UserOperations at once. An attacker can pay almost no fees while dumping free computation on bundlers, making it computationally infeasible to maintain a mempool containing only valid UserOperations. Also, if spam criteria differ from node to node, nodes may end up treating each other as spammers, splitting the network, so a shared validation rule across all nodes is needed.

In a proxy structure, where several functional modules share one storage, different modules can write to the same location and overwrite each other's data. In March 2020 the Solidity compiler made it possible to place a struct at an arbitrary location in storage, which gave rise to the Diamond Storage pattern, where a readable string is hashed to determine the location, and it became widely used through ERC-2535 Diamonds. However, this approach was not a formal standard for a long time. ERC-7201, published in 2023, standardized a pattern with the same purpose but proposed a different calculation formula from the Diamond Storage already in use. As a result, existing implementations in production did not receive the protection of a standard. This standard codifies the simple, proven original method so that new projects can use it, and it also recognizes past implementations as compliant.

In upgradeable contracts, adding a state variable during an upgrade can affect the storage locations of existing variables, which makes adding variables difficult. 1nti7qwtwvp: When a CCIP Read-aware contract calls another contract that may also implement CCIP Read, it must catch every OffchainLookup thrown by the other contract and revert with a different error if sender differs from the other contract's address. It may also replace every OffchainLookup with a different error, which avoids implementing nested support but makes nested lookups impossible. The default nested-call error propagation in Solidity must not be left as is. If A calls B, which does not know CCIP, and B calls A back so that A throws OffchainLookup, then B and A propagate it in turn, and an error whose sender matches A and looks valid reaches the client, but in reality only the inner call completes. 1o3ncpcwyx7: A Soulbound Token is an NFT that is bound to one account and cannot be handed to anyone else. The Ethereum community has wanted tokens that cannot be transferred and whose value comes from social meaning, like bound items in World of Warcraft. But there was no standard for this, so many developers implemented it by simply raising an error when a user calls the transfer function. For a wallet or app, there is no way to know in advance which tokens cannot be transferred, and each implementation works differently, so they are hard to use together. 1ohh1xqc5gi: A diamond is a structure that provides the functionality of multiple implementation contracts through a single contract address, and it was first standardized in ERC-2535. However, the existing approach required collecting the identifier of each function (the function selector) off-chain and passing them in whenever a diamond was deployed or upgraded. General development tools such as Hardhat and Foundry do not support this selector management by default, so developers had to depend on separate scripts or third-party libraries. Passing and storing the selector list as call data also increased gas costs. This standard mandates an exportSelectors() function through which a facet reports its own selectors on-chain. This moves selector collection onto the chain and handles deployment and upgrades per facet. As a result, off-chain selector management disappears, deployment becomes more deterministic, and gas efficiency improves.

1p0ft1y0w51: On a blockchain, anyone can see the contents of a transaction before it is processed. Actions that need secrecy, such as voting, therefore expose their contents and suffer harms such as front-running, where someone sees another party's transaction and jumps ahead of it, back-running, where someone follows right behind it, and sandwich attacks, which wrap a transaction on both sides. The long-standing remedy is commit-reveal. You first submit only the hash of the content to lock in a commitment, then reveal the original later to have it verified. However, if each standard, such as voting standards and token standards, designs its own commit scheme, they are incompatible with one another. This standard fixes a single commit function as the common piece and leaves the reveal method to each application, so commit-reveal can be added anywhere without changing the function signatures of existing standards.

1p5svk87vc5: EIP-712 is a way of signing structured messages. To prevent replay attacks, where a signature is reused elsewhere, and to reduce phishing, it uses a domain separator that binds a signature to a domain such as a specific contract. The domain consists of a name, version, chain ID, verifying contract address, and optional fields such as a salt, but EIP-712 itself does not define how a contract can announce which fields it uses and with what values. As a result, apps had to fit the domain separately for each contract, and generic integration was impossible. The original text points out that even EIP-2612 (permit), known to greatly improve user experience, has not been widely adopted for this reason. The DOMAIN_SEPARATOR function of EIP-2612 returns only a hash value, so it cannot be used to show the user the domain contents and verify them before signing. This standard fills the gap by defining an interface through which an app can read a contract's domain definition.

1plx4kod4gs: Today, once an NFT is sold, it leaves the hands of the original issuer and can be resold endlessly to anyone. In some situations, however, this unlimited transferability is a problem. NFTs whose value rests on scarcity, such as premium auction items or limited editions, are exposed to frequent resale. Game items that should wear out after a few uses, and memberships and licenses that should be transferable only a set number of times, are hard to implement with standard methods. There is also no simple mechanism to curb adversarial arbitrage that repeats within a short time, such as ultra-short-term trading, or the practice of repeatedly restaking NFT positions to build leverage. This standard defines a common interface that sets a transfer limit per token, counts actual transfers, and blocks transfers that exceed the limit, enabling this kind of fine-grained transfer restriction while staying compatible with ERC-721.

1sn3l0hlfsw: The SECP256k1 curve is defined by y^2 = x^3 + 7 (mod p), with p = 2^256 - 2^32 - 977, and G is the generator point. The recipient holds the private keys p_spend and p_view and the corresponding public keys P_spend and P_view, and publishes the meta-address. generateStealthAddress computes in the following order. Create a 32-byte random ephemeral private key p_ephemeral and derive the ephemeral public key P_ephemeral. Parse P_spend and P_view from the meta-address. Compute the shared secret s = p_ephemeral · P_view and hash it to get s_h = h(s). The view tag v is the most significant byte of s_h, s_h[0]. Compute S_h = s_h · G and then the stealth public key P_stealth = P_spend + S_h. The stealth address a_stealth is pubkeyToAddress(P_stealth). The function returns a_stealth, P_ephemeral, and v.

This function matches KeyGen in the IETF BLS signature standard draft, so the same seed produces the same key, and it has been reviewed by many cryptographers. Digital assets such as files, however, do not lose quality when copied and can be held by many people, and the sole-ownership model cannot capture this. Passing ownership strips the original owner of their rights, so a structure in which several people jointly own the same asset cannot be built in a standard way. The standard also has no mechanism for the party who first provided an asset to keep earning rewards as it circulates afterward. This standard supports joint ownership by adding the new owner to a list on transfer instead of removing the existing owner, and it sends a set fee to the provider on every transfer so that creators and providers are rewarded. Also, if membership is split only into member and non-member, it is hard to naturally express tiered benefits that vary with holdings or voting power proportional to holdings. ChainType is a 2-byte value corresponding to a CASA namespace, and it determines how the following ChainReference and Address are interpreted and displayed. A UserOperation that accesses the sender address of another UserOperation in the same bundle, or whose validation accesses an address created by a factory for another UserOperation, must be excluded, and for each paymaster the bundler must track whether the deposit covers all of its UserOperations. After building the bundle, it runs debug_traceCall with the maximum gas to verify the opcode and storage access rules and the whole handleOps transaction, and uses the gas consumed for the actual transaction. If it reverts, the entity that the EntryPoint called last with CALL in the trace is taken as the cause (it does not assume FailedOp), and the corresponding UserOperation is removed from the bundle and the mempool. If the cause is a factory or paymaster and the sender is not staked, that factory or paymaster is blocked, and if the sender is staked, the sender is blocked instead. This is repeated until debug_traceCall succeeds. This presupposes a reputation system that throttles or temporarily bans global entities (paymasters and factories) that invalidate multiple UserOperations, and stake is required to prevent Sybil attacks. Stake is not enforced on-chain; each bundler checks it during simulation, and staked entities get relaxed storage usage limits. Because UserOperations from unrelated senders can enter the same transaction, contracts that use EIP-1153 transient storage must clean up on their own any transient storage used for sensitive information or access control.

1zcqmcpniau: There are many kinds of cross-chain messaging protocols (bridges) that pass messages between chains, and they differ in their degree of decentralization, their architecture, and the properties they guarantee. The problem is that almost every protocol uses a different interface and workflow. As a result, moving a contract built for one bridge to another bridge is practically impossible, and building general-purpose contracts that rely on cross-chain communication is also hard. A contract tied to a single bridge becomes exposed to risk if that bridge halts or is deprecated. This standard defines a common interface and flow for sending and receiving messages, so that existing protocols can be used in the same way through adapter contracts. Its goal is to make bridges easier to swap and combine, and to reduce vendor lock-in.

1zhts00ok4v: An Ethereum signature consists of three values, r, s and yParity, totaling 65 bytes. On chain, however, data is handled in 256-bit (32-byte) units, so fitting a 65-byte signature to that unit inserts 31 zero-padded bytes and makes it 96 bytes. When a transaction is encoded with RLP, the yParity value also takes up 1.5 bytes on average by itself. This waste repeats when verifying the origin of a transaction sent by an externally owned account (EOA), and also when verifying signatures on chain, as in meta-transactions or multisig contracts. 20z9vjmljor: To call a contract on Ethereum, the sending account must hold ETH to pay for gas. A meta transaction is a scheme in which a third party pays the gas on behalf of a user who has no ETH. The user only signs the request, and a Gas Relay submits that request as an actual transaction. The problem is that the caller the contract sees (msg.sender) is the relay that paid for gas. A contract that does not know about meta transactions cannot tell who actually signed, and cannot stop a relay from forging, altering, or replaying a request. Without a standard interface, wallets and apps also have no way to find out which contracts accept meta transactions or which forwarders they trust. As a result, every contract has to build its own logic for safely receiving requests.

21bh9b7vtd0: checkStealthAddress works using only the viewing private key p_view and the spending public key P_spend. It multiplies the announcement's ephemeral public key by p_view to get the shared secret s = p_view · P_ephemeral and computes s_h = h(s). It compares s_h[0] with the announcement's view tag, and if they differ the announcement is not yours, so the remaining computation is skipped. If they match, it computes S_h = s_h · G, P_stealth = P_spend + S_h, and a_stealth = pubkeyToAddress(P_stealth), and returns true if this matches the announcement's stealth address. computeStealthKey uses both the viewing private key and the spending private key p_spend. After obtaining s_h the same way, it computes the stealth private key as p_stealth = p_spend + s_h. Because deriving the private key requires the spending private key, the viewing key alone can only confirm receipt.

26lc23aoab6: An atomic swap using a Hash Time Lock Contract (HTLC) lets two parties swap tokens without an intermediary, but it gives the party who initiates the trade an optionality: they can freely choose whether to go through with the exchange over a period of hours. The initiator can watch exchange rate movements during that window and only complete the trade when it favors them, simply abandoning it otherwise. This is effectively the same as a financial American call option, yet the initiator pays no premium for that option, leaving the counterparty unilaterally disadvantaged. Conversely, properly harnessing this optionality makes it possible to construct a call option product without any trusted third party. This standard defines a common way for protocols to implement this by locking the premium into the contract alongside the swap, removing the arbitrage opportunity and preventing either side from maliciously locking up the other's funds.

28m1koousjh: There is a design in which a single token is used in two forms at once: ERC-20 (fungible token) and ERC-721 (non-fungible token, NFT). For example, acquiring ERC-20 automatically mints NFTs in proportion to the holding, which makes fractional ownership of NFTs possible using only standard tokens. But without a standard way to verify from outside that two contracts are linked, decentralized exchanges and NFT marketplaces cannot show the relationship between the two tokens on screen. 2fisjrp7s98: Without a view tag, the recipient must perform 2 elliptic curve multiplications (ecMUL), 2 hashes, and 1 elliptic curve addition (ecADD) for every announcement they check. With a view tag, most announcements are filtered out by hashing the shared secret and comparing only the first byte, so only 1 ecMUL and 1 hash are needed, and parsing time drops by about 6 times. Because the view tag is 1 byte, the probability of skipping the remaining computation for an announcement that is not yours is 255/256. In exchange, 1 byte of the shared secret is revealed, so the security margin falls from 128 bits to 124 bits. This reduction affects only privacy and does not affect the security of stealth address generation itself. The authors describe this as a tradeoff in which view tags improve off-chain efficiency at the cost of making the announcement event more complex.

2g2lzedvpem: The sequential nonce in the Ethereum protocol is used for replay protection and ordering, but it is too restrictive for an account that wants to define its own ordering rules. This standard splits a single uint256 nonce into two values, a 192-bit key and a 64-bit sequence. The value is stored in the EntryPoint and read with getNonce(sender, key). The sequence is validated in the EntryPoint for each key, and if validation fails the UserOperation is invalid and the bundle is reverted. The sequence increases monotonically and sequentially per sender, and a new key can be introduced at any time with an arbitrary value, with its sequence starting at 0. This guarantees the on-chain uniqueness of the UserOperation hash while letting an account layer any logic it wants on the key field. A bundler is recommended to start validation with a getNonce call, and to accept multiple UserOperations from the same sender it must track the key and sequence pairs already in the mempool. To enforce a classic sequential nonce, the validation function performs require(userOp.nonce<type(uint64).max). To set up a separate channel for administrative operations, implement a check that the key is ADMIN_KEY when the first 4 bytes of callData are ADMIN_METHODSIG, or otherwise that the key is 0.

This means an NFT is merely an item that sits inside a wallet and cannot be used like a wallet. As a result, it is difficult to represent with a single NFT real-world assets such as a game character that accumulates equipment and abilities over time, a car composed of multiple parts, an investment portfolio holding multiple assets, or a membership card that accumulates usage history. Attaching item tokens to a character NFT requires building a separate contract mechanism each time, and transferring the attached assets along with the NFT when it is sold is also cumbersome. This standard aims to give every NFT the same rights as an Ethereum user. It does this by assigning each NFT a dedicated account address computed deterministically, and giving control of that account to the NFT's holder.

5xh8r6hk7l: Tokenizing real-world assets such as securities or real estate brings regulation with it. Transfers may need to be allowed only to permitted users, and assets may need to be frozen and forcibly moved for law enforcement. Existing token standards such as ERC-20, ERC-721, and ERC-1155 have no structure to carry these requirements. As a result, each issuer attached compliance features in its own way, and a decentralized finance (DeFi) protocol that wanted to integrate with RWA tokens had to learn each token's different approach individually. Earlier attempts at a universal RWA standard enforced fine-grained role-based access control, mandatory on-chain allowlists, specific on-chain identity systems, and metadata handling, which imposed unnecessary complexity and gas costs even on simple use cases that need none of those features. The assets are also so varied that a single comprehensive framework that specifies everything is hard to build. What was needed was a minimal common interface that leaves implementation to each party and unifies only the outward appearance.

The simplest way to protect these is ownership-based access control, which concentrates all permissions in a single owner account. Role-based access control, by contrast, assigns one or more roles to multiple users and grants access to privileged functions based on role. Following the principle of least privilege, necessary permissions can be split among multiple people, making this approach safer and more flexible than ownership-based control. However, when each contract implements role management differently, it becomes hard for wallets or tools to read the permission structure in a consistent way. This standard defines a single common interface for reading, granting, creating, and removing roles, and for expressing role metadata.

However, the existing intent standards ERC-7521 and ERC-7683 define only flows initiated by a single party and do not specify how to verify that multiple parties have actually agreed. As a result, projects building multi-party tasks had to design their own agreement verification methods, and each also had to guard against signatures being reused elsewhere (replay) and participant lists being manipulated. This standard fills that gap with the smallest possible onchain mechanism. It gathers the proposer's EIP-712 signed intent and each participant's acceptance signature, and unifies the rules so that the intent becomes executable only when all required acceptances have been collected and are valid.

e3phu5z0du: The original text explains why each element was removed from ERC-1155. First, mandatory callbacks are a burden for implementers who do not need callbacks or want to use their own mechanism, so they were removed. This reduces contract size, gas, and complexity. Second, batch processing is useful, but it is better decided per implementation than fixed in the standard. In environments such as rollups, where calldata is written to global storage, the calldata layout may need to be arranged differently. Third, the names safeTransfer and safeTransferFrom are misleading, because in practice they make an external call to a recipient account that has code and hand execution flow to an arbitrary contract. Removing both the mandatory callbacks and the word safe makes the default control flow safer. Fourth, because some methods are missing, it is not backward compatible with ERC-1155, but wrappers for ERC-20, ERC-721, and ERC-1155 can be built.

The direct lookup, implementsERC165InterfaceNoCache, sends three staticcalls through noThrowCall, each with 30000 gas. First, the supportsInterface(0x01ffc9a7) call must succeed and return a nonzero value. Second, the call for the invalid ID 0xffffffff must succeed and return 0. A contract that changes its interfaces dynamically must update the cache manually with updateERC165Cache(_contract, _interfaceId). The hook is called at the very end of the transfer, after balances are updated and events are emitted. If it accepts the transfer, onERC1155Received returns 0xf23a6e61 and onERC1155BatchReceived returns 0xbc197c81, and to reject it reverts. This initialization function must also be callable only from entryPoint.senderCreator(). The EntryPoint cannot tell whether initialization has already happened and so may call it multiple times, so it is best to allow it only once. udl2lw0kjo: A UserOperation is a structure that carries the action to be sent on behalf of a user. To avoid confusion it is not called a transaction. Like a transaction, it has nonce, callData, maxFeePerGas, maxPriorityFeePerGas, and signature. It also has sender (the account sending the action), factory and factoryData (the address and data of the factory that creates a new account, or the 0x7702 flag for an EIP-7702 account), callGasLimit (gas for the execution call), verificationGasLimit (gas for the verification step), preVerificationGas (extra gas paid to the bundler), and paymaster, paymasterVerificationGasLimit, paymasterPostOpGasLimit, and paymasterData (paymaster fields). How the signature is interpreted is decided by the account contract implementation, not by the protocol. To prevent replay across chains or across EntryPoint versions, the signature must depend on the chainid and the EntryPoint address. On-chain, a compressed PackedUserOperation is used, which bundles initCode (the factory address concatenated with factoryData, or EIP-7702 data), accountGasLimits (verificationGasLimit as 16 bytes concatenated with callGasLimit as 16 bytes), gasFees (maxPriorityFeePerGas as 16 bytes concatenated with maxFeePerGas as 16 bytes), and paymasterAndData (the paymaster fields concatenated). An EIP-7702 authorization tuple can be passed along with the UserOperation, but it is not included in the struct itself.

There is almost no ability to delegate subdomains, and there is only one record type, so multiple resources cannot be attached to the same name. ur7404pcme: Like a computer filesystem where folders contain folders and files, many services use hierarchical structures. eBay's categories, Reddit's boards and posts, and Twitter's lists are all examples. However, the existing NFT standard EIP-721 treats each token as independent, so there is no way to express which token belongs under which. To put such relationships on-chain, each project has to build its own approach, and external programs such as wallets and apps have no common way to read the structure. uvtyfyhuz5: To complete an ownership transfer, the new owner must perform mutual authentication with the asset. It is done off-chain with the asset and on-chain with the token. Using the elliptic curve secp256k1 and the base point P, the owner creates a secret key SK_O_A and a public key PK_O_A = SK_O_A * P, then computes the shared key K_O = PK_A * SK_O_A from the asset's public key PK_A. The asset computes K_A = SK_A * PK_O_A with its own secret key, and mathematically the two values are equal. The token stores the public data needed for the agreement in dataEngagement and the hashes of the shared keys in hashK_OA and hashK_UA, and the asset, owner and user must verify that they are using the correct shared secret key. Because a new session key is created for each authentication, the asset's trustworthiness can be traced even when the owner and user change.

xjkfh3a0th: ERC-1155 is a multi-token standard in which one contract handles multiple kinds of tokens distinguished by id. However, base ERC-1155 has no function that tells how many tokens of a given id have been issued in total. So even when a wallet or app wanted to know the total quantity of a token, there was no standard way to rely on. In practice, implementations that report supply, such as OpenZeppelin's ERC1155Supply, were already in use, but unless the function names and behavior are fixed by a standard, readers cannot safely write common code. z3x0l5shyl: Security validation logic in smart contracts is usually bundled inside the contract body itself. When code such as access control or input checks is fused together with business logic, the code becomes tightly coupled, making it hard to examine or fix security issues in isolation. Changing a single check requires touching the entire contract, and well-built validation logic is difficult to reuse as-is in other contracts. The software industry widely uses a middleware pattern, wrapping a call with common pre- and post-processing checks under the same call signature, but smart contracts lacked a common interface for this kind of insertion. ERC-7746 defines a standard hook interface called before and after function execution, separating security checks into an independent layer that can be composed or upgraded as needed.
